fetid

/FET-id/ - the stress falls on FET · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fetid means giving off a strong, foul smell.

A fetid haze hung over the flooded crawl space, where a month of standing water had steeped in the dark.

Example

The courthouse cistern had been sealed since the fifties, and the surveyor who finally cracked the hatch reeled back off the ladder. Below him lay sixty years of trapped water — black, still, skinned with scum — and fetid air that had been breathing only itself since Eisenhower. He taped the hatch open and gave it two days before anyone went down.

Fetid is the exact word for that air, because it means giving off a strong, foul smell — and the word leans hard toward staleness gone rotten: shut-in rooms, standing water, spaces the wind never rinses. Musty is the closet's mild complaint; stuffy is merely unrefreshed. Fetid says the stillness itself has gone foul.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

reeking: Reeking says a strong smell is actively pouring off something — and it can be any smell at all, even perfume or gasoline. Fetid is narrower and darker: the foulness of shut-in air and standing water, stale places gone rotten. A locker room reeks; a sealed cellar is fetid.

stinking: Stinking is the plain, everyday word for smelling bad, at home anywhere from a gym bag to a garbage truck. Fetid adds the shut-in, unmoving note — air or water that has stood in the dark until the stillness itself turned foul.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fresh: clean and newly aired

airy: open and breathable

Where it sits · how unbearable the air becomes — stuffy → fetid → suffocating

stuffy vs. fetid: Stuffy air is merely close and unrefreshed — it wants an open window, nothing worse — and it sits far below fetid, where the stillness itself has gone foul.

suffocating vs. fetid: Suffocating goes further than fetid — fetid air revolts the people breathing it; suffocating air can barely be breathed at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fet

Root — fet: to stink (Latin fetere)

Suffix — -id

Suffix — -id: adjective ending: in a given state, as in humid

Put it together

Put it together: Fet- (stink) + -id (in that state) = in a state of stinking. The -id family of adjectives all name settled conditions — humid air, vivid color — and fetid joins them: not a stray whiff but air that has settled into foulness.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin fetere, "to stink," left almost nothing else behind in English — only fetor, a term physicians use for a diagnostic odor, and that is this word's own close kin rather than a new relative. The memory hook is the suffix instead: -id words name standing states, and fetid names the state of stinking.

Strength Check

Word Choice

literary / pungent

Fetid is for airless, standing places — trapped air, still water, rooms the wind never reaches. Its unit-mates split the territory: putrid is the smell of flesh and food actively decaying, rancid belongs to fats and oils gone over, and noisome is the broadest — offensive or outright harmful, smelly or not. If the scene is a swamp, a bilge, or a sealed basement, fetid is your word.
